name: generic
description: GDPR-pattern red flags that apply to any service: how long data is kept, who it goes to, whether you are being profiled, and whether you can say no.
reference: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), read as a set of general expectations rather than as a jurisdiction claim

metadata.note: These rules describe patterns, not legal conclusions. A finding here means a user should read a clause, not that a company is breaking the law.

rules.reason: This service keeps your data indefinitely. There is no point at which it is deleted.
rules.note: Storage limitation requires data to be kept no longer than necessary for the stated purpose. 'Indefinitely' and 'perpetual' are the explicit failures of that principle. Wikimedia's 'Non-Personal Information may be retained indefinitely' was flagged; non-personal, anonymised and aggregate data are excluded.

rules.reason: How long your data is kept is described only as 'as long as necessary', with no actual period given.
rules.reference: GDPR Art. 13(2)(a), the retention period must be stated
rules.note: Very common and not by itself alarming, which is why it is low. It becomes meaningful in combination: a service that will not say how long it keeps data and also shares it with third parties has told you very little. Real policies rarely say 'indefinitely'. Google says 'We keep some data until you delete your Google Account', which is a retention statement with none of the retention vocabulary a pattern list would guess.

rules.reason: This service sells or rents your personal information to other companies.
rules.reference: GDPR Art. 6, lawful basis; Art. 13(1)(e), recipients
rules.note: The negation list matters more than the patterns here. Most policies mention selling data specifically in order to promise they do not: Fibe's live policy reads 'We do not sell, rent, lease your Personal Information to anybody and will never do so.' Paytm's 'Not to sell your Personal Data to any third party' was flagged as a sale until 'not to sell' was a negation. Microsoft's 'Data brokers from which we purchase demographic data' described buying data and was flagged as a sale; a broker now only counts next to a selling or sharing verb.

rules.reason: Your information is passed to third parties such as partners, affiliates or advertisers.
rules.note: Sharing is normal and often necessary; the reason line says what happens rather than accusing anyone. Legal-obligation disclosures are negated out because a policy cannot promise not to answer a court order. The verb list was too narrow. 'We work with third-party service providers' and 'We may receive information from advertisers and other data partners' are both disclosures a reader wants, and neither used a verb we matched. Fired on every one of 20 real policies, including Signal and Proton, so it carried no information. Proton's 'No user data is ever shared with third parties' was flagged until that form was a negation, and Groww's scope sentence 'This Privacy Policy does not apply to information ... collected by any third-party' likewise. Sharing with processors acting for the service is now low; sharing with advertisers is caught by gdpr.tracking.targeted_ads. A clause that is a question (a section heading such as 'DOES PAYTM SHARE PERSONAL DATA WITH THIRD PARTIES?') states nothing and is ignored.
rules.hedge_reason: Your information is passed to companies that work for this service, such as payment processors or hosting providers.

rules.reason: This service builds a profile of your behaviour and uses it to make decisions about you.
rules.reference: GDPR Art. 4(4), profiling; Art. 22, automated decision-making
rules.note: Automated decision-making is singled out by Art. 22 because it affects people without a human ever looking. In a lending context this is also how a credit decision gets made about someone with no recourse. Bare 'profile' was removed as a pattern: it matched 'add a profile picture' and 'Changing Your Profile Name And Picture', which are account settings, not profiling.

rules.reason: You are tracked across other websites and apps, not just while using this one.
rules.reference: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a), transparency; ePrivacy Directive Art. 5(3)
rules.note: Tracking that follows a user off the property is the thing people are least likely to expect and most likely to object to.

rules.reason: Your data is used to target advertising at you.
rules.reference: GDPR Art. 21(2), the right to object to direct marketing
rules.note: Art. 21(2) gives an unconditional right to object. Worth surfacing precisely because the opt-out usually exists but is buried. DuckDuckGo's 'Microsoft has committed to not associate your ad-click behavior with a user profile' was flagged until 'committed to not' was a negation. Sharing with advertisers moved here from third_party, which now treats processors as low.

rules.reason: What you upload here is used to train the company's AI models. Your photos, files or messages become training data.
rules.note: This is the permission-purpose mismatch case: a camera permission granted so you can take a picture, and a policy elsewhere that quietly repurposes the picture as training data. Purpose limitation is the principle being stretched, and the granting of the permission is not where the user finds out.

rules.reason: Simply using the service is treated as your agreement. You are not actually being asked.
rules.reference: GDPR Art. 4(11), consent must be freely given and unambiguous
rules.note: Consent by continued use is not consent under Art. 4(11). Live example: Fibe's policy reads 'By using the Application, you signify your consent to our use of cookies.' Low rather than medium in the generic set: it is the standard opening of nearly every policy. rbi.consent.bundled stays high for lenders, where explicit consent is required.

rules.reason: The company can change these terms whenever it likes, without telling you first.
rules.note: Live example: Kissht's terms read 'We reserve the right to update or modify the Terms of Use at any time, without prior notice, at our sole discretion.' Terms you agreed to once are not the terms you are held to later. No longer matches a bare 'at any time' or 'reserve the right to change', which nearly every policy says; the reason is about changes made without telling the user, and that is what is matched.

rules.reason: Your data is sent to servers in other countries, where different privacy laws apply.
rules.reference: GDPR Chapter V, transfers to third countries
rules.note: Not wrong in itself, and Chapter V exists to make it lawful. Reported so a user knows which legal system is actually protecting their data. Low rather than medium: almost every service hosts abroad, and safeguards such as Standard Contractual Clauses were being reported as risks.

rules.reason: The company states it cannot guarantee your data is secure.
rules.note: Near-universal boilerplate and honest in its way, which is why it is low rather than medium. Included so the absence of it is also visible.

rules.reason: This policy never explains how to opt out, withdraw consent, or delete your data. There is no stated way to say no.
rules.reference: GDPR Art. 7(3), the right to withdraw consent; Art. 17, erasure
rules.note: Absence is the finding, so this rule is document-scoped: no individual clause is wrong, the document as a whole is missing something a reader needs. Art. 7(3) requires withdrawing consent to be as easy as giving it, which is impossible if the policy never says how. Medium rather than high in the generic set: a minimal-collection service such as Signal has little to opt out of, and a legal page that links to a separate privacy centre was getting an alarming finding. Lenders keep rbi.consent.no_withdrawal at high.
